inline.s: O monks, a mind of flattery and sycophancy (bending to please others) runs contrary to the Way. Therefore, you should make your mind upright. Know that flattery and sycophancy serve only to deceive oneself and others; for one who cultivates the Way this is absolutely impermissible. Therefore you should correct your mind and take straightforwardness as its foundation.

[Straightforwardness] Zhi means upright; 'straightforwardness' is rectitude. An upright mind has no flattery or sycophancy. The Buddha Way lies in awakening to the innate naturalness originally possessed by all beings; this mind is the root of all practices. [Correcting the mind] To correct and solemnize one's own mind.

Master Ouyi said: 'Words that flatter and seek to please are called sycophancy; thoughts that bend and waver with circumstances are called crookedness. Sycophancy is not straightforwardness, and crookedness is not uprightness. One only deceives oneself and also deceives others; such a person is by no means one who has entered the Way. An upright mind is the place of practice; because the heart's words are straight, it never has any crooked appearance. If one lacks right mindfulness of true reality, how can one be called "correcting the mind"?'

[O monks, know that a person of many desires seeks gain lavishly and therefore has much suffering and distress; a person of few desires seeks nothing and wants nothing, and so is free of this affliction. Even the simple state of few desires is worth cultivating, how much more so when few desires can give rise to all manner of merit! A person of few desires does not flatter and bend to win others' approval, nor is he drawn along by his faculties. One who practices few desires is calm and open, with no anxiety or fear. Whatever he encounters, he has abundance and is never in want. One who has few desires attains Nirvana. This is called having few desires!]

O monks, you should know that a person of many desires, because he seeks gain lavishly, has much suffering and distress; a person of few desires seeks nothing and wants nothing, so he is free of this affliction. Since even the simple state of few desires is free of this affliction, one should already cultivate few desires; how much more so when few desires can give rise to all manner of merit and accomplish countless holy and wholesome dharmas! A person of few desires does not flatter and bend to please others, nor is he dragged along by the five faculties into attachment to the five desires. One who practices few desires contends with no one, seeks nothing in the world, and so his mind is broad and open, at ease and natural, with no worry or fear. In whatever circumstances he always has abundance and never feels want. One who is able to have few desires can realize Nirvana. This is why one should have few desires!

[O monks, if you wish to free yourselves from all suffering and distress, you should contemplate contentment. The practice of contentment is the abode of wealth, happiness, and peace. A contented person, though he lies upon the ground, is still at ease and joyful; one who is discontent, though he dwells in heaven, is still not satisfied. The discontented, though rich, are poor; the contented, though poor, are rich. The discontented are ever dragged by the five desires and are pitied by the contented. This is called contentment!]

O monks, if you wish to free yourselves from the many kinds of suffering and distress, you should contemplate contentment. The practice of contentment is the abode of wealth, happiness, and peace. A contented person, though he sleeps on the ground, still feels joy and peace; one who is discontent, though in heaven, is never satisfied. The discontented, though wealthy, always feel want; the contented, though poor, always feel rich. The discontented are ever dragged by the five desires to create karma and receive retribution, and are pitied and sighed over by the contented. This is why one should be contented!
[An-yin (secure)] It means stable and secure. Here 'yin' is the same as 'wen' (stable).
To have few desires is to seek nothing outwardly; to be contented is to be inwardly fulfilled.

[O monks, if you seek stillness and the peace of non-doing, you should depart from turmoil and dwell alone in quiet. The person of quiet places is honored and respected by Shakra and all the gods. Therefore, you should give up your own followers and the followers of others, and in solitude contemplate how to extinguish the root of suffering. One who delights in crowds receives the afflictions of the crowd; for example, a great tree on which many birds gather is in danger of withering and breaking. Those bound in the world sink into the mass of suffering, like an old elephant trapped in mud, unable to free itself. This is called dwelling far from turmoil!]

O monks, if you seek stillness and have the peace of non-doing, you should depart from noise and dwell alone. The person of quiet solitude is honored by Shakra and all the gods. Therefore, you should leave your own followers and the followers of others, and in solitude contemplate the root of extinguishing suffering. One who delights in being among people contracts the afflictions of people; for example, a great tree on which many birds nest is liable to wither and break. In this way one is bound by the world and sinks into the mass of suffering, like an aged elephant trapped in a swamp, unable to struggle free. This is why one should stay far from turmoil!

[Kui-nao (turmoil)] Uproar and clamor. [Xian-ju (dwelling in quiet)] Dwelling alone in one place. [Di-shi (Shakra)] The lord of the Trayastrimsa heaven. [Di-shi zhu tian (Shakra and the gods)] Shakra and the heavenly gods. [One's own group and others] 'One's own group' means one's own teacher, students, and companions; 'others' means the circle of outsiders. [Contemplating the extinction of the root of suffering] To contemplate uprooting suffering at its very root, far from its cause. [An old elephant sunk in mud] Like an aged elephant sinking in a swamp; the 'old elephant' is a metaphor for one worn out by the tangle of external conditions.
The Ten Virtues of Dwelling in Quiet
1. No encounters between men and women, no heart of lust; 2. No occasion for idle talk, no fault of false speech;
3. No enemies to face, no fear of quarrels; 4. No friends of right and wrong, no error of praise and blame;
5. No seeing others' failures, no speaking of others' faults; 6. No trailing after kinsfolk, no attachment to family;
7. No persons face to face, no vexation of etiquette; 8. No arriving guests, no feasting and entertaining to manage;
9. No dealing with crowds, no hope of fine clothes; 10. Alone in the practice of the wondrous way, free from all other hindrances.

[O monks, if you are diligent and vigorous, nothing is difficult for you. Therefore, you should be diligent and vigorous, for example, as a small stream that flows constantly can wear through stone. If the mind of a practitioner relaxes and falters again and again, it is like drilling for fire and resting before the wood is hot; though you want to obtain fire, fire is hard to obtain. This is called vigor!]

O monks, if you cultivate the Way diligently and vigorously, nothing can stand against you. Therefore, you should be diligent and vigorous, just as drops of water falling ceaselessly can drip through stone. If a practitioner's mind is often slothful and neglectful, this is like drilling wood for fire and resting before the wood becomes hot. Drilling and stopping, stopping and drilling, though you wish to draw out fire, the fire will not come. This is why one should be diligently relentless!
[Shuo-shuo (again and again)] Repeatedly; often.
That water drips through stone is entirely due to the merit of unceasing persistence.

[O monks, seeking a good spiritual friend, seeking good protection and aid, nothing is like not forgetting mindfulness. For one who does not forget mindfulness, the thieves of the afflictions cannot enter. Therefore, you should always hold mindfulness gathered in the mind. If mindfulness is lost, all merit is lost. If the power of mindfulness is firm and strong, though you enter among the thieves of the five desires, you are not harmed by them, just as one who dons armor and enters the battle line has no fear. This is called not forgetting mindfulness!]

O monks, seeking the instruction of a good spiritual friend and seeking the protection and aid of good devotees are both beneath not forgetting right mindfulness. For one who does not forget right mindfulness, the thieves of the afflictions cannot intrude. Therefore, you should always hold right mindfulness gathered in the mind. If right mindfulness is lost, all merit is lost. If the power of right mindfulness is firm and strong, though you enter among the thieves of the five desires, you are not harmed by them, just as one who wears armor and enters the enemy line has no fear. This is why one should not forget right mindfulness!

[Not forgetting mindfulness] Not forgetting right mindfulness. [Right mindfulness] The thought of the true Dharma, for example the Buddha-name of a reciter of the Buddha, the mantra of one who holds a mantra, or the huato of one who meditates in Chan. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana says: 'If the mind runs scattered, then gather it back and dwell in right mindfulness.'
Not forgetting right mindfulness is the foremost of all practices.

[O monks, if you gather the mind, the mind becomes concentrated. Because the mind is in concentration, it can know the characteristics of arising and ceasing in the world. Therefore, you should always diligently cultivate the concentrations. One who attains concentration has a mind that does not scatter. For example, a household that treasures water well manages its dikes and ponds; a practitioner is likewise. For the sake of the water of wisdom, he cultivates meditation well, so that it is not lost. This is called concentration!]

O monks, if you can gather your scattered thoughts, then you can rest the mind on one object and attain concentration. Because the mind is in concentration, it can clearly discern the characteristics of arising and ceasing in the world. Therefore, you should always diligently cultivate the various concentrations. One who attains concentration has a mind that is not scattered. Just as a farm household that treasures water well manages its dikes and ponds, so too a practitioner, for the sake of treasuring the water of wisdom, cultivates meditation well, so that the water of wisdom is not lost. This is why one should gather the mind and enter concentration!

Master Ouyi said: 'When the mind is in concentration, it is like the bright sun hanging in the sky, clearly illuminating all things, and so it can know the characteristics of arising and ceasing in the world.'

[Concentration] Resting the mind on a single object without letting it scatter is called concentration. [Characteristics of arising and ceasing] The characteristics of the world are nothing else but the phenomena of arising and ceasing, ceasing and arising, this arising-and-ceasing and ceasing-and-arising without end; therefore they are called the characteristics of arising and ceasing.

[O monks, if you have wisdom, you have no clinging and attachment. Always examine yourself and do not let it be lost; thus, in my Dharma you can gain liberation. If it is not so, you are neither a cultivator of the Way nor a layperson, and you are nothing at all. A person of true wisdom is a sturdy ship for crossing the sea of old age, sickness, and death; he is a great bright lamp in the darkness of ignorance; he is the good medicine for all the sick; he is the sharp axe that fells the tree of the afflictions. Therefore, you should increase your own wisdom through the wisdom of hearing, the wisdom of reflection, and the wisdom of practice. If a person has the illumination of wisdom, though he has no divine eye, he is a clear-sighted person. This is called wisdom!]

O monks, if you have wisdom, you will not cling and be attached. Therefore, you must always examine yourself and not let wisdom be lost; this way, in my Buddha-Dharma you can gain liberation. If it is not so, you are neither a renunciate cultivating the Way nor a layperson studying Buddhism, and you are nothing at all. Full and solid wisdom is the sturdy treasure-ship for crossing the great sea of old age, sickness, and death; it is the great bright lamp in the darkness of ignorance; it is the good medicine for all the sick; it is the sharp axe that fells the tree of the afflictions. Therefore, you should increase your wisdom through hearing, reflection, and practice. If a person has the illumination of wisdom, though he has no divine eye, he is a clear-sighted person. This is why one should never lose wisdom!

[A person of true wisdom] 'Real wisdom' means full and solid wisdom. 'Zhe' (one who) here is a modal particle that marks a pause in tone and forms a sentence of judgment. For example: Chen Sheng, (he) was a man of Yangcheng. [Wisdom of hearing, wisdom of reflection, wisdom of practice] The wisdom of hearing, the wisdom of reflection, and the wisdom of practice. The wisdom of hearing is the wisdom born from hearing the Dharma; the wisdom of reflection is the wisdom born from reflecting on Buddhist principles; the wisdom of practice is the wisdom born from diligent cultivation of meditation.

[O monks, through all kinds of idle talk the mind becomes disturbed; though one has left home, one has not yet gained release. Therefore, monks, you should quickly abandon the idle talk that disturbs the mind. If you wish to attain the joy of still extinction, you must well put an end to the affliction of idle talk. This is called not speaking idly!]

O monks, in speaking and hearing all kinds of idle talk, the mind becomes disturbed; though you have left home, in fact you have not yet freed yourselves from the bonds of the world. Therefore, you should immediately abandon the idle talk that disturbs the mind. If you wish to attain the joy of still extinction, you must well put an end to this calamity of idle talk. This is why one should not speak idly!
[Idle talk] Erroneous and meaningless speech. That is, speech that opposes truth, merely disturbs the mind and wastes time, and cannot increase wholesome dharmas.

[O monks, toward all these merits, you should always be single-minded, renouncing all negligence as you would flee a vengeful enemy. The benefits spoken by the great compassionate World-Honored One are all complete and ultimate; you should only diligently practice them. Whether in the mountains, in a desolate marsh, beneath a tree, or in a quiet chamber, be mindful of the Dharma you have received and do not let it be lost. Always encourage yourselves and practice diligently; do not die in vain and afterwards regret. I am like a good physician who knows the illness and prescribes the medicine; whether you take it or not is not the physician's fault. I am also like a good guide who leads people onto the good path; hearing it yet not practicing is not the fault of the guide.]

O monks, toward all the merits and dharmas spoken above, you should practice them with a single mind, renouncing all negligence as you would stay far from a vengeful enemy. I, the great compassionate World-Honored One, have spoken of the dharmas that benefit liberation, and they are all the path of ultimacy; you must diligently practice them. Whether in the mountains, in a desolate marsh, beneath a tree, or in a quiet chamber, hold to the Dharma you have received and do not let it be lost. Always encourage yourselves and practice diligently; do not waste your whole life in vain and then regret. I am like a good physician who knows your illness and tells you the remedy; whether you take it or not is beyond the physician's responsibility. I am also like an excellent guide who leads you along the golden road of liberation; but you do not follow, and this is not the fault of the guide.
[Negligence] Letting the mind run loose and acting willfully and wantonly.

blocks.text: 22. The Four Noble Truths Encompass All

inline.s: [If any of you have doubt about the four truths of suffering and the rest, you should ask at once; do not harbor doubt and fail to seek resolution. At that time the World-Honored One thus proclaimed three times, and no one asked. Why? Because the assembly had no doubt.]

If any of you still have doubt about the four truths of suffering, its origination, its cessation, and the path, you can ask at once. Do not harbor doubt and fail to seek an answer. At that time the World-Honored One thus loudly asked three times, yet no one asked. Why? Because everyone had no doubt.

[The four truths] These are the four noble truths: the truth of suffering, the truth of origination, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path. 'Di' (truth) means truth. First, the truth of suffering explains the truth that life is full of suffering. Suffering is characterized by oppression. Life has the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, and countless sufferings; suffering is the truth of actual life. Second, the 'ji' of the truth of origination means bringing about or creating; it is the truth that explains the cause of suffering, that is, where the pain of life comes from. The suffering of life arises because craving produces karma, and so one suffers and transmigrates. Third, the truth of cessation explains the truth of extinguishing all suffering. When all the origination of suffering, that is, craving, is cut off forever without remainder, without defilement and without attachment, one no longer suffers or transmigrates; this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, the truth of the path explains how to extinguish forever the origination of suffering, that is, craving, which is the path that ends suffering, the eightfold noble path. Among the four noble truths, origination is the cause and suffering is the fruit; the path is the cause and cessation is the fruit.

[The three sufferings] The suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of conditioned existence. The suffering of suffering: people already have a body of birth and death, which is suffering enough; on top of that the many sufferings press upon them, so that suffering is added to suffering; hence it is called the suffering of suffering. The suffering of change is the suffering felt when an occasionally appearing blissful state is lost. The suffering of conditioned existence is the suffering of all conditions being impermanent, flowing on without rest, and never settled. [The eight sufferings] First, the suffering of birth, the pain at birth; second, the suffering of old age, the pain of aging and weakness; third, the suffering of sickness, the pain of illness; fourth, the suffering of death, the pain at the moment of death; fifth, the suffering of separation from the loved, the pain of parting from what one loves; sixth, the suffering of meeting with the hated, the pain of encountering those one resents; seventh, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, the pain of wishes unfulfilled; eighth, the suffering of the blazing of the five aggregates, that is, the fierce burning activity of the five aggregates covering over true nature.

[The eightfold noble path] Also called the eightfold right path, the eight paths of the noble ones: first, right view, correct seeing and understanding; second, right intention, correct thinking; third, right speech, correct words; fourth, right action, correct conduct; fifth, right livelihood, correct occupation and way of life; sixth, right effort, correct striving; seventh, right mindfulness, correct awareness; eighth, right concentration, correct meditation. Cultivating this eightfold noble path, one can realize the fruit of Arhatship.

[Then Aniruddha, observing the minds of the assembly, said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! The moon can be made hot, and the sun can be made cold, but the four truths spoken by the Buddha cannot be changed. The Buddha says the truth of suffering is truly suffering and cannot be made pleasure; origination is truly the cause, with no other cause; if suffering is extinguished, then the cause is extinguished, and because the cause is extinguished the fruit is extinguished; the path that extinguishes suffering is truly the true path, with no other path. World-Honored One! These monks are certain and without doubt regarding the four truths.]

Then Aniruddha, observing the minds of the assembly, reported to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Even if the moon can be made hot and the sun can be made cold, the four truths spoken by the Buddha cannot be altered. The Buddha speaks of 'suffering': this is real suffering and cannot be turned into pleasure; 'origination' is the real cause of suffering, with no other cause; to extinguish suffering one must extinguish this cause of origination; the 'path' that extinguishes this cause of origination is truly the true path, with no other path. World-Honored One! We monks are now certain and without any doubt about the four truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path.
[Aniruddha] That is Aniruddha, one of the Buddha's ten great disciples, renowned as foremost in the divine eye.

[Among this assembly, those whose task is not yet accomplished, seeing the Buddha's passing, will certainly grieve. Those newly entered into the Dharma, hearing what the Buddha has said, will all be saved; for example, seeing lightning in the night, they immediately see the Way. Those whose task is accomplished and have crossed the sea of suffering only have this thought: how swift indeed is the World-Honored One's passing!]

Aniruddha continued: Among the assembly present, those who have not yet severed the afflictions, seeing the Buddha's passing, will certainly feel sorrow and grief. Those newly entered into the Dharma, hearing what the Buddha has said above, will all be saved, for having heard this instruction, it is as if a flash of lightning appeared in the dark night, and they clearly see the path of liberation. Those arhats whose task is accomplished have already crossed the sea of suffering and no longer transmigrate; they only think: how swift indeed is the World-Honored One's passing!

[Task not yet accomplished] This refers to those of the first, second, and third fruits, whose afflictions are not yet wholly cut off. [Task accomplished] The arhat's afflictions are wholly cut off and he has escaped birth and death; therefore it is said his task is accomplished.

Aniruddha spoke of the three types of people in the assembly: first, those whose task is not yet accomplished, whose delusions of thought are not yet wholly cut off, and who therefore feel grief; second, those newly entered into the Dharma, who, hearing what the Buddha has said above, have clearly seen the path of liberation and will all be saved; third, the arhats whose task is accomplished, whose delusions of view and thought are wholly cut off, so they no longer have grief of affection, and they think: how swift indeed is the World-Honored One's passing!

[Although Aniruddha said these words, the whole assembly fully understood the meaning of the four noble truths. The World-Honored One, wishing to make this great assembly all firm and steadfast, in his great compassion again spoke to them: O monks, do not harbor grief and affliction. Even if I dwelt in the world for an eon, in the end I would also pass away; meeting without parting can never be obtained. The dharmas for benefiting oneself and benefiting others are all complete; if I remained long, there would be no further benefit. Those who can be saved, whether in heaven or among men, have all been saved; for those not yet saved, the causes and conditions for their salvation have already been established. From now on, my disciples practicing it in turn, this is how the Tathagata's Dharma body remains present and does not pass away.]

Although Aniruddha said these words, the assembly present fully understood the meaning of the four noble truths. The World-Honored One, wishing to enable them all to gain a firm and steadfast mind for the Way, in his great compassion again instructed the assembly: O monks, do not grieve and be afflicted. Even if I dwelt in the world for an eon, in the end I would enter into cessation; to meet and never part is impossible. The dharmas for benefiting oneself and benefiting others you already possess, and you can practice the Way relying on them. If I remained longer, there would be no further benefit. Those who can be saved, whether in heaven or among men, I have already saved; for those not yet saved, I have already planted the causes and conditions for their salvation. From now on, my disciples practicing the Way in turn, saving themselves and saving others, this is how the Tathagata's Dharma body remains present and does not pass away.

blocks.text: 25. All Things in the World Are Impermanent

inline.s: [Therefore, know that all things in the world are impermanent; meeting must be followed by parting. Do not harbor grief and affliction; such is the nature of the world. Be diligent and vigorous, and seek liberation early; with the light of wisdom, extinguish all the darkness of delusion. The world is truly perilous and fragile, with nothing firm and lasting. I now gain cessation, as one removes a dire illness. This is the body to be relinquished, a thing of sin and evil, falsely called a body, sunk in the great sea of old age, sickness, birth, and death. What wise person, being able to destroy it, would not rejoice as one who kills a vengeful enemy!]

Therefore, know that everything in the world is impermanent; where there is gathering there must be scattering. Do not harbor grief and affliction; such are all the phenomena of the world. Therefore, you should be diligent and vigorous, seeking liberation as early as possible, and with the light of wisdom extinguish all the darkness of ignorance and delusion. The world is truly perilous and fragile, with nothing firm and lasting. Today I enter cessation, as one removes a dire illness. This physical body is a body to be relinquished; it is a thing of sin and evil, falsely called a body, sunk in the great sea of old age, sickness, birth, and death. What wise person, being able to destroy this body, would not rejoice, as one who kills a vengeful enemy!

[O monks, always be single-minded and diligently seek the path that leads out of the world. All dharmas of the world, moving and unmoving, are all marks of decay and unrest. You should now stop; say no more. The time is about to pass; I wish to enter cessation. This is my final instruction.]

O monks, always be single-minded and diligently seek the noble path that leads out of birth and death. All dharmas of the world, moving and unmoving, are marks of decay and unrest. You should stop speaking; say no more. The time of the middle of the night is nearly past; I must enter Nirvana. These are my final instructions.

[Moving and unmoving dharmas] The desire realm is the moving dharma; the form realm and the formless realm are the unmoving dharmas. Though there is this distinction of moving and still, they all belong to impermanence and non-self, so one cannot but think of escaping them. [The three realms] The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The desire realm is the world where beings with the two desires of sex and food dwell; from the six desire heavens above, through the four great continents where humans and animals live, down to the Uninterrupted Hell, all belong to it. The form realm is the world where beings free of the two desires of sex and food but still having form dwell; the eighteen heavens of the four dhyanas belong to it. The formless realm is the world where beings with neither form dwell, abiding their minds and consciousness in profound meditation; the four heavens of the immaterial sphere belong to it. These three realms are the spheres through which ordinary beings transmigrate in birth and death; therefore Buddhist practitioners take leaping out of the three realms as their aim.

Master Ouyi said: 'This final instruction is precisely the display of the testamentary teaching, the most excellent and most essential of all the dharmas that maintain the Dharma. Alas! This last earnest counsel is the utmost compassion! As a disciple, how should one not carve it into the marrow of one's bones and engrave it upon the liver!'
